analysis.title: Where does last week's selloff stand in history, and what's driven bigger ones?
key_insights: Despite Monday's recovery, last week's selloff was one of the bigger declines of recent years. On Friday the S&P 500 entered correction territory for the first time since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff.
On the same Friday US HY spreads reached their widest since April 2025 and the VIX closed above 35 again.

No sudden reassessment of the growth outlook this time, unlike the 2020 pandemic and 2025 Liberation Day. DB economists see global growth at 3.5% in 2027 and US growth slowing by only a tenth to 2.3%.

No meaningful data deterioration, unlike summer 2024 (ISM miss, Sahm rule breach) or 2015-16. November flash PMIs were mostly robust, with German composite at a 4-year high of 55.0, Euro Area steady at 51.7 and US composite at 54.6.

No hawkish repricing like 2022. Hikes are priced in, but 66bps are priced by the September 2027 meeting versus 82bps on October 6 when the S&P 500 hit its record high, so pricing has shifted slightly dovishly.

Bear markets of the last 50 years (S&P 500 down 20% or more) have coincided with at least one of a recession, widespread recession expectations, or a multi-hike Fed tightening cycle. None applies now.
The dot com parallel is questioned because that bust came with a broader slowdown. The S&P 500 peaked March 2000 but only entered bear market territory in March 2001 as the recession began.

The last bear market without those three factors was arguably the 1962 Kennedy Slide, when the S&P 500 fell 28% peak to trough from December 1961 to June 1962 on valuation concerns. Conditions today would be historically unusual for a bear market.
Stress is concentrated in tech, with specific concerns around an AI slowdown rather than an exogenous shock or policy shift.

sector_views.rationale: Stress in tech tied to AI slowdown fears, but the macro backdrop lacks the recession or tightening conditions that accompanied past bear markets.

tension_points.bull_case: No growth reassessment, data deterioration or hawkish repricing, which have accompanied bear markets for 60 years, so a bear market would be historically unusual.
tension_points.bear_case: Stress in tech and dot com parallels, with the possibility of data deterioration and financial stress feeding into the real economy. The 1962 Kennedy Slide shows valuation concerns alone can drive a 28% fall.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sudden growth reassessment, meaningful data deterioration (such as a Sahm rule breach or ISM contraction), or a hawkish central bank repricing.

theme_stances.key_argument: Bear markets have required a recession, recession expectations or Fed tightening, none of which is present now.
theme_stances.evidence: the present conditions would be historically unusual ones for a bear market to occur
